title: Best Lottery Game to Play: A Dollar-for-Dollar Compare
description: Odds, ticket costs, prize tiers, and expected value across Powerball, Mega Millions, NY Lotto, Take 5, and Millionaire for Life. You decide.
content:
What Makes a Lottery Game Worth Playing

Before declaring any game the best lottery game to play, it helps to define what "best" actually means — because the answer depends entirely on what you're optimizing for. A player chasing a life-changing nine-figure jackpot is making a fundamentally different calculation than someone who wants the highest probability of winning anything on any given day. Both are legitimate goals. They just point to very different games.

Five criteria drive this comparison: ticket cost (what you spend per entry), jackpot odds (the probability of hitting the top prize), secondary tier odds (the probability of winning a smaller prize), draw frequency (how often you get a shot), and jackpot structure (lump sum versus annuity, and how large the top prize typically runs). Each criterion tells a different part of the story. The table below puts all five in front of you at once.

Side-by-Side Comparison: Five Games, One Table

The figures below reflect current game structures as of October 2026. Jackpot sizes are approximate and fluctuate between draws. Odds are fixed by each game's format and do not change regardless of jackpot size or ticket sales.

GameTicket PriceJackpot OddsOverall Odds (Any Prize)Draw FrequencyTop Prize Structure
Powerball$2.001 in 292,201,3381 in 24.93x/weekLump sum / annuity, $20M+ minimum
Mega Millions$5.001 in 302,575,3501 in 242x/weekLump sum / annuity, $20M+ minimum
NY Lotto$1.001 in 45,057,4741 in 462x/weekPari-mutuel lump sum, variable

The jackpot odds gap between Powerball and Take 5 is roughly 507 to 1. A single Take 5 ticket gives you approximately 507 times better odds of hitting its top prize than a Powerball ticket gives you of hitting its jackpot — at half the ticket price.

Cost-Per-Chance Analysis: What Does Each Dollar Actually Buy?

Comparing raw odds ignores ticket price. A game with worse odds but a lower ticket cost may deliver better value per dollar spent depending on which prize tier you're targeting. The metric here is cost per unit of probability — specifically, what you pay for one unit of jackpot probability and one unit of any-prize probability.

Powerball

At $2.00 per ticket and jackpot odds of 1 in 292,201,338, each dollar spent at Powerball buys approximately 3.42 billionths of a jackpot chance. Overall odds of winning any prize sit at roughly 1 in 24.9. The Power Play multiplier (an additional $1) can increase non-jackpot prizes but does not affect jackpot odds. Across 2,015 draws in our database, Powerball frequency statistics show number #42 appearing 14 times in the last 100 draws — but that historical data has no bearing on future probability.

Mega Millions

The April 2025 ticket price increase to $5.00 significantly changed Mega Millions' cost-per-chance profile. With jackpot odds of 1 in 302,575,350, each dollar now buys approximately 0.66 billionths of a jackpot chance — making it the most expensive path to a jackpot attempt among all five games on a per-dollar basis. Secondary prizes did increase with the price change, and overall odds of any prize sit near 1 in 24. The Megaplier option adds cost without improving jackpot odds. Readers interested in historical number patterns can explore Mega Millions frequency statistics across 2,551 draws.

NY Lotto

NY Lotto's $1.00 ticket and jackpot odds of 1 in 45,057,474 place it in a middle tier — far better jackpot odds than either national game, at half or less of the ticket cost. Each dollar buys approximately 22.2 billionths of a jackpot chance, which is roughly 6.5 times more jackpot probability per dollar than Powerball and about 33 times more than Mega Millions at its new price. The tradeoff is a pari-mutuel structure: jackpot size varies with ticket sales and is split among all winners, so actual payouts are less predictable. Overall odds of winning any prize are approximately 1 in 46 — the least favorable secondary odds of the five games.

Take 5

Take 5 is the outlier in this comparison. At $1.00 per ticket with jackpot odds of 1 in 575,757 and overall any-prize odds of approximately 1 in 8.77, it delivers more probability per dollar than any other game in this analysis across both metrics. Each dollar buys roughly 1,738 millionths of a jackpot chance. The top prize is modest — typically ranging from $10,000 to $50,000-plus depending on ticket sales — and is pari-mutuel. But with two draws per day and a Take 5 database spanning 12,684 draws, it is the most data-rich game here and offers the most frequent entry points at the lowest per-entry cost.

Millionaire for Life

At $2.00 per ticket with jackpot odds of 1 in 3,838,380, Millionaire for Life sits between NY Lotto and Take 5 on the probability spectrum. Each dollar buys approximately 130 millionths of a jackpot chance. Overall any-prize odds of approximately 1 in 7.76 are the most favorable of any game here. However, the top prize — $1,000 per week for life — is structured as a lifetime annuity rather than a lump sum, which creates a fundamentally different expected value calculation. The present value of that annuity depends on the winner's age and a discount rate applied to future payments. The game has only 244 draws in our database, limiting the reliability of any long-term trend analysis compared to more established games.

Each Game's Unique Advantage

  • Powerball: Largest typical jackpot floors, widest national availability, nine prize tiers, and three draws per week provide more annual entry points than Mega Millions.
  • Mega Millions: The single largest jackpots in U.S. lottery history have come from this game. For players whose only goal is maximum possible prize ceiling, it holds the record.
  • NY Lotto: The lowest-cost path to a multi-million-dollar jackpot attempt among these five games. One dollar buys roughly 6.5 times more jackpot probability than the same dollar spent on Powerball.
  • Take 5: Best overall odds, lowest ticket price, twice-daily draws, and the most extensive historical draw database of any game tracked here — 12,684 draws provides substantially more pattern data than any other option.
  • Millionaire for Life: The only game here that pays its top prize as recurring income rather than a single payment. For players who would prefer a structured income stream over a lump sum, no other game in this comparison offers that structure at the top tier.

The Tradeoffs: Choosing the Right Game for Your Goals

Answering the question of the best lottery game to play requires knowing your own criteria first. The data above does not point to a single answer — it points to different answers for different objectives.

If your goal is maximum jackpot size, Mega Millions and Powerball are the only games in this comparison capable of producing nine-figure prizes. You pay for that possibility with the worst jackpot odds and, in Mega Millions' case, the highest ticket price. Every dollar spent on either national game buys significantly less jackpot probability than the same dollar spent on any regional game here.

If your goal is best odds of winning anything, Take 5 and Millionaire for Life offer overall prize odds that are three to five times better than the national games. Take 5's 1-in-8.77 overall odds on a $1 ticket represent the most probability-efficient entry in this comparison for non-jackpot prizes.

If your goal is a jackpot attempt at the lowest cost, NY Lotto provides multi-million-dollar jackpot odds at $1 per ticket — cheaper than Powerball, Mega Millions, or Millionaire for Life, and with better jackpot odds than all three.

If your goal is frequent play opportunities, Take 5 draws twice daily and Millionaire for Life draws daily — both provide far more annual draw opportunities than the twice-weekly NY Lotto or the three-times-weekly national games.

If you are drawn to income-style prize structures rather than a single payout, Millionaire for Life is the only game here built around that format. Keep in mind that with only 244 draws in the database, long-term statistical patterns for this game are less established than for the others.

None of these advantages cancel each other out cleanly. Take 5's superior odds come with a capped prize. Mega Millions' massive jackpot potential comes with the worst per-dollar probability of any game here. NY Lotto's low cost comes with pari-mutuel variability and the weakest secondary prize odds. The tradeoffs are real, and the right weighting depends on what you're actually trying to get out of the experience. For readers who want to dig further into number frequency data before making any decisions, Powerball number analysis and Mega Millions number analysis are available with full draw histories.
